newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone - diamonds, poverty, strife.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone - diamonds, poverty, strife.

text.p: Sierra Leone, where army soldiers said they had seized power in a coup on Sunday, is one of the poorest countries on earth and yet has yielded some of the finest diamonds ever mined.

A former British colony that grew out of a settlement founded for freed slaves 200 years, it has been gripped by civil unrest since 1991 and clashes continue despite a November 1996 accord. Life expectancy is the world's lowest -- 39 years.
POPULATION: 4.4 million (1994 U.N. estimate) Ethnic groups: Temnes, Limbas, Lokos, Korankos, Mendes, Kissis, Konos, Creole.
RELIGION: About 70 per cent traditional African beliefs, 25 per cent Moslem, five per cent Christian.
LANGUAGES: English is the official language but a Creole version known as "Krio" is the lingua franca. There are many other local languages, including Mende and Temne.

LAND AREA: Sierra Leone covers 71,740 square km (27,700 square miles). Fronting the Atlantic Ocean, its neighbours are Guinea to the north and east and Liberia to the southeast. The climate is tropical.

ARMED FORCES: (International Institute for Strategic Studies, The Military Balance 1995-96) Total: 6,200. Army -- 6,000, four infantry battalions, two artillery battalions and a contingent of 700 serving with West African peacekeepers in Liberia. Navy -- 200-strong with coastal patrol boats. Nigerian troops (1,000) and Guinean troops (300) back the army.

ECONOMY: Average per capita income of about $150 a year (1993 U.N. estimate); 1993 Gross National Product $635 million (World Bank estimate). Annual inflation between 1985 and 1993 averaged over 70 percent but has since fallen. External debt totalled $1.38 billion in 1993 (World Bank estimate). Diamonds, gold, iron ore, bauxite and titanium, a strategic metal used in planes and rockets, account for about two-thirds of foreign exchange income.

RECENT HISTORY: Sierra Leone became independent on April 27, 1961. Veteran president Siaka Stevens quit in 1985 and chose former army chief Joseph Momoh as successor. Momoh won 99 percent of the vote in a presidential election that year. Stevens died in 1988. Parliament approved a draft multi-party constitution in 1991 but the start of a rebel war postponed implementation. Captain Valentine Strasser, 27, seized power in 1992 vowing to end the war. Rebels, who held 17 Western hostages for several months, stepped up operations at the end of 1994 and attacked heavily guarded approaches to Freetown in 1995. The arrival of private South African military trainers helped turn the tide in the army's favour but resulted in no outright victory. Sierra Leoneans turned out in force for presidential and parliamentary elections in February 1996 despite attacks by rebels or soldiers keen to hang onto power. Lawyer Ahmad Tejan Kabbah's party emerged as the largest in the new 80-seat parliament with 27 seats. He himself won a March 15 presidential election runoff. He took over from Strasser's successor General Julius Maada Bio and signed a peace deal with Foday Sankoh, leader of the rebel Revolutionary United Front, in Abidjan on November 30, 1996. Isolated clashes continued and intensified recently.
